title: Māori Settlement of Aotearoa
titleline: Māori Settlement of Aotearoa - The History Web
para1: Maori Settlement of Aotearoa. The Maori settlement of Aotearoa (New Zealand) came when Polynesian voyagers arrived by canoe in several waves between 1250 and 1300 CE, guided across the Pacific by the brilliance of the stars in their waka hourua - voyaging canoes - from the ancestral homeland of Hawaiki. The first centuries are remembered as the 'Moahunter' or colonization period (1280-1500 CE), when the settlers adapted their tropical traditions to a cooler, temperate land and developed a distinct tribal culture organized around intricate wood carving, genealogical memory, and the fiercely independent warrior tradition for which the Maori became renowned.
para2: Society was structured around the iwi, the tribe, and sacred knowledge was carried by respected specialists: the tohunga ta moko, the tattoo craftsman, was considered tapu, and the moko itself - reserved for the face and for Maori of high social status, for the head was considered the most sacred part of the body - chronicled a person's ancestral and life history, indicating their whakapapa, the line of ancestors from whom they descended; ta moko is related to the tatu of Eastern Polynesia and the tatau of Samoa, a tradition extending back thousands of years. The arrival of Europeans from the late eighteenth century - explorers, traders, and collectors - brought new relationships and new pressures. In 1840 the relationship was formalized by the Treaty of Waitangi, New Zealand's founding document: negotiated at Waitangi on February 5-6 by Britain's designated consul and lieutenant governor William Hobson, it was ultimately signed by 540 Maori rangatira, or chiefs. That same year Britain annexed all of New Zealand - the North Island on the basis of the treaty, and the South Island by the, in this case dubious, right of discovery.
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Traditional Maori Tattoo of New Zealand

title: Pre-unification Hawaiian Chiefdoms
titleline: Pre-unification Hawaiian Chiefdoms - The History Web
para1: Pre-Unification Hawaiian Chiefdoms. Before 1795, the Hawaiian Islands were divided into competing chiefdoms, each island ruled by its own ali'i - chiefly lines such as the 'Ewa ali'i of Oahu and the ali'i nui of Hawaii island - contesting land, status, and power across the archipelago. Contact with Europeans, beginning when Captain Cook anchored off Kauai, introduced firearms, ships, disease, and new goods into these old rivalries. Into this world was born Kamehameha, whose rise legend aligned with the predicted reappearance of Halley's comet; as a teenager he was said to have overturned a great sacred volcanic boulder, and in 1779 he is believed - though accounts vary - to have fought in the conflict in which Cook was killed. When the ruling chief, his uncle, died in 1782, the dispute over how his lands would be distributed incited a bloody civil war, and at the Battle of Moku'ohai Kamehameha came face-to-face with his cousin and prevailed.
para2: Kamehameha then fought a generation of wars, facing his rivals with small, elite groups of warriors rather than single decisive battles. He adopted the muskets and ship cannon that came with the growing number of Anglo merchants in the islands - though scholars such as Paul D'Arcy caution that their role has been overstated, for his power rested as much on alliances, trade, and the favor of the war god, sealed when he finished erecting the great temple of Pu'ukohola Heiau in 1791. In 1795, at the epic Battle of Nu'uanu, he conquered Oahu and unified most of the islands, establishing the Kingdom of Hawaii; after two failed assaults on Kauai, he completed the unification in 1810 not by conquest but by a historic peace meeting, in which his longtime rival King Kaumuali'i of Kauai agreed to recognize his rule. The old patchwork of warring chiefdoms had been transformed into a centralized monarchy.

title: Rapa Nui (Easter Island) Culture
titleline: Rapa Nui (Easter Island) Culture - The History Web
para1: Rapa Nui (Easter Island) Culture. Rapa Nui is one of the most remote inhabited places on Earth - a volcanic island in the southeastern Pacific, some 1,400 miles west of South America. The date of its first settlement is actively debated: older accounts placed colonization between 400 and 800 AD, but newer radiocarbon analyses of the earliest layers - notably the work of Terry Hunt and Carl Lipo - point to settlement around 1200 AD, a shorter chronology reinforced by a meta-analysis of more than 1,400 dates across East Polynesia, though some researchers still question the dismissal of the older dates. What is agreed is that colonists from an unidentified homeland in Eastern Polynesia reached the island after sailing in a southeasterly direction for many weeks. There they created a highly organized ceremonial culture centered on ancestor veneration, famous worldwide for the moai: colossal stone figures carved as images of ancestral chiefs whose supernatural power protected the community. This society matters because its artistic achievements - and the pressures that later transformed it - offer one of the most compelling studies in human adaptation and resilience in the entire Pacific.
para2: Most moai were carved from soft volcanic tuff at Rano Raraku, an extinct crater that served as the primary statue quarry, then moved to their final destinations on wooden sleds or rollers - a feat modern archaeologists have experimentally recreated - and erected on temple platforms (ahu) along the coast, facing inland to keep watch over the local communities; they range from 8 feet to an unfinished example over 70 feet high. When Europeans arrived in 1722 the moai tradition was already in decline, and by the mid-nineteenth century all the statues had fallen. The islanders also invented rongorongo, a system of writing first described by the missionary Eugene Eyraud in 1864 and never deciphered - research suggests it was invented independently, without influence from European writing systems. A devastating Peruvian slave raid in 1862, followed by smallpox epidemics, reduced the population catastrophically; Chile annexed the island in 1888 and leased it to a sheep-ranching company that confined the islanders to one village for decades - yet they held fast to their language, their memory, and their pride in the ancestors who raised the moai.

title: The Saudeleur Dynasty & Nan Madol
titleline: The Saudeleur Dynasty & Nan Madol - The History Web
para1: The Saudeleur Dynasty & Nan Madol. The Saudeleur Dynasty was the centralized dynasty that ruled the island of Pohnpei in Micronesia from around 1100 to about 1628, governing from Nan Madol - the so-called 'Venice of the Pacific', an apt comparison, for like Venice the city rests on a network of canals and waterways, though unlike Venice it is built around artificially constructed islets. Off the southeast coast of Pohnpei, ninety-nine artificial islets rise on walls of basalt columns and coral boulders, harboring the remains of stone palaces, temples, tombs, and dwellings; the great edifices were built between 1200 and 1500 CE as the ceremonial center of the Saudeleur, a vibrant period in Pacific Island culture. The dynasty matters because the huge scale of Nan Madol - a royal city raised upon the reef itself - is one of the most audacious achievements of the ancient Pacific.
para2: The Saudeleur concentrated political and religious power at the capital, where the mortuary sector sprawls across fifty-eight islets in the northeast around a colossal royal tomb; the elite occupants of the islets depended on their subjects even for fresh water. The tribute system began seasonally - seafood presented to the Saudeleur at designated times - but over time the dynasty's demands grew oppressive, drawing the resentment of the Pohnpeians. The dynasty ended with the invasion of Isokelekel, a semi-mythical foreigner who, in Pohnpeian tradition, knew his destiny of vengeance even in the womb: accounts differ - in one, a game between local children and those from Isokelekel's canoe escalated into open war; in another, he staged an insurrection after winning the trust of his hosts - but all agree he overthrew the Saudeleur and replaced their rule with a new order. Nan Madol was abandoned, and today its ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage site.
source2label: World History Encyclopedia: Nan Madol, Reconstructed
source3label: Humanities LibreTexts: 5.4: Nan Madol- “In the space between things”

title: The Tu'i Tonga Empire
titleline: The Tu'i Tonga Empire - The History Web
para1: The Tui Tonga Empire. The Tui Tonga Empire was the maritime power centered on Tongatapu that dominated large swathes of Polynesia for centuries. In about 950 AD the first Tui Tonga, 'Aho'eitu, began to expand his rule outside of Tonga, and the line of sacred kings and queens known as the Tui Tonga ruled from at least the tenth century, their throne set by the lagoon at Lapaha. The empire's success was based largely upon its Imperial Navy, and under Tui-ta-tui, the eleventh Tui Tonga, it reached its height of expansion, with tributes said to be exacted from all the tributary chiefdoms; its influence ranged widely through East 'Uvea, Rotuma, Futuna, Samoa, and Niue, and reached into parts of Micronesia, Vanuatu, and New Caledonia. The Manu'a islands of Samoa were considered sacred by the early Tongan kings.
para2: The empire's decline began with numerous wars and internal pressure: in the 13th or 14th centuries the Samoans expelled the Tongans from their lands, and later Tui Tonga kings - several of them the sons of Samoan noblewomen - presided over an empire increasingly Samoan in orientation - Tongan scholars describe this later form of the empire as 'Samoanized', importing many Samoan policies and titles. The sacred kings also shed their worldly burdens: in approximately 1470 the reigning Tui Tonga transferred his temporal powers to his brother, who held the title of Tui Ha'a Takalaua, and around 1600 a similar transfer created a third line, the Tui Kanokupolu - founded for the half-Samoan Ngata - which divided regional rule between them and, as time went on, eclipsed the ancient sacred line. The Tui Tonga survived as a spiritual dignity while real power passed to the newer dynasties from which the modern Tongan monarchy descends.
source2label: UNESCO: Returning to the Lau Islands, all sails out

title: The Yap Empire (Micronesia)
titleline: The Yap Empire (Micronesia) - The History Web
para1: The Yap Empire. The 'Yap Empire' was the name given to a maritime trading and tribute network centered on the island of Yap in Micronesia, which from around 950 AD - when the village of Gatcheper became its seat - held suzerainty over islands and atolls stretching over 1,300 kilometers to the east, from Ngulu to Ulithi and from Fais to Namonuito. Small and informal compared with other marine empires, it was held together not by garrisons but by the sawey tribute system: regular tributes known as pitigil tamol, presented to the chief of Wanyan village and to the chief of Gatchaper, the paramount chief of Gagil, traveled from east to west - from as far as Namonuito to Ulithi and finally to Yap - in the form of lavalava cloth and other island wealth. Yap is equally famous for its rai, the great stone money: discs so large that when they were exchanged within the island, people hardly bothered to move them - they simply remembered who owned what, and the rai stayed put.
para2: The outer islanders of the network held the same social ranking as Yapese serfs on the main islands and were expected to show deference to their Yapese overlords, while smaller, localized systems of trade and tribute among Lamotrek, Satawal, and Elato persisted into the 1950s. Yap itself was drawn into the colonial world: rediscovered by the Spanish galleon captain Francisco Lazeano in 1686, it passed to Germany in 1899 - the era when the American trader David O'Keefe built his own trading empire by importing stone money from Palau in return for copra - and after the First World War passed to Japan as a League of Nations mandate, administered from Japan's South Seas headquarters at Koror. When the great canoe fleets that once assembled at Ulithi to carry the tribute could no longer sail, the old network faded and the sawey system declined - but the rai remain the enduring symbol of Yap's singular place in Pacific history.

title: The Tahitian Chiefdoms
titleline: The Tahitian Chiefdoms - The History Web
para1: The Tahitian Chiefdoms. The Tahitian chiefdoms (c. 1000-1815) ruled the largest and richest island of eastern Polynesia. Settled from islands to the west in the last great wave of Polynesian voyaging, Tahitian society grew around the ariki, hereditary chiefs who traced their descent from the gods and whose power was displayed at the marae, open-air temples of stone where priests conducted the rituals that bound chiefs, gods, and people. District chiefs ruled the valleys and coasts of Tahiti, bound together and divided by kinship, alliance, and war.
para2: Tahitian society was elaborate and strongly ranked. Great chiefs commanded war canoes and armies, collected tribute in food, cloth, and prized red feathers, and patronized the famous arioi, traveling companies of performers dedicated to the god Oro, whose cult spread from island to island. Life centered on the districts, each with its marae and its ruling family, and European visitors in the eighteenth century, from Wallis to Bougainville and Cook, described a fertile island of breadfruit, coconut palms, and a populous, sophisticated people.
para3: The age of the independent chiefdoms ended in the era of European contact. One district family, the Pomare line, rose above the rest with the help of European guns: Pomare I unified much of Tahiti and its neighbors in the 1790s, and his son Pomare II, converted by Protestant missionaries, completed the conquest and in 1815 founded the Kingdom of Tahiti, a Christian monarchy that ruled until the French protectorate of 1842.
para4: The chiefdoms left Tahiti its language, its chiefly families, and its marae, many of them still standing. Their history captures the whole arc of Polynesian experience, from the first settlement of the islands through the flowering of chiefly civilization to the shock of European arrival, when old rivalries and new weapons and religions together transformed the Pacific world.
source2label: University of Hawaii Press: Ancient Tahitian Society: The Emergence of the Pomares

title: The Chamorro and the Marianas
titleline: The Chamorro and the Marianas - The History Web
para1: The Chamorro and the Marianas. The Chamorro (c. 1500 BC - 1721) are the indigenous people of the Mariana Islands in the western Pacific, the first humans to settle so far into the open ocean. They reached the Marianas around 1500 BC, voyaging thousands of kilometers from Island Southeast Asia, and for three thousand years they developed one of the most distinctive societies of the Pacific in isolation, farming, fishing, and sailing between their islands in swift outrigger canoes that astonished the first Europeans.
para2: Ancient Chamorro society is best known for its monumental stone pillars, the latte. Rows of these pillars, capped with heavy bowl-shaped stones, supported the wooden houses of chiefs and important families in villages across the islands; the largest latte stones, on Tinian, tower over five meters high. The latte period, from about a thousand years ago until Spanish contact, was the classical age of Chamorro culture, a ranked society organized in matrilineal clans, rich in shell ornaments, red-slipped pottery, and stone and shell tools.
para3: The arrival of Europeans shattered this world. Magellan reached the Marianas in 1521, and in 1668 Spanish missionaries and soldiers began the conquest and conversion of the islands. The Chamorro resisted in a series of wars, but superior weapons and, far more terribly, newly introduced diseases destroyed them: the Chamorro population, perhaps fifty thousand at contact, collapsed to a few thousand by 1720, and the survivors were concentrated in mission villages on Guam.
para4: The Chamorro survived the catastrophe and rebuilt their identity. Their language, their latte stones, their clan traditions, and their memory of resistance endure among their descendants in the Marianas today, and the story of their settlement and survival is central to the history of the Pacific.
source3label: Micronesica Journal: An Overview of Latte Period Archaeology
source4label: Guam Visitors Bureau: Ancient Latte Stones of Guam

title: The Tui Manu'a and the Samoan Chiefdoms
titleline: The Tui Manu'a and the Samoan Chiefdoms - The History Web
para1: The Tui Manu'a and the Samoan Chiefdoms. The Tui Manu'a and the Samoan chiefdoms (c. AD 500-1909) represent one of the oldest political traditions of Polynesia. Samoa was settled by Lapita voyagers around three thousand years ago, and out of its early communities grew a society of chiefs, the matai, who governed villages and districts through councils bound by elaborate custom, the fa'a Samoa, the Samoan way. The most exalted title of all was the Tui Manu'a, the sacred ruler of the Manu'a islands, whose authority Samoan tradition placed at the very beginning of the islands' history.
para2: The Tui Manu'a was more than an ordinary chief. According to Samoan oral tradition, the title descended from Tagaloa, the supreme god, and its holders ruled not only Manu'a but at times claimed tribute and allegiance across Samoa and even beyond, to Fiji, Tonga, and other island groups; some traditions remember a great Samoan maritime confederacy reaching across the southwest Pacific. Archaeology confirms Samoa's wide ancient connections, and the prestige of the Manu'a title was acknowledged far beyond its home islands.
para3: From the thirteenth century the balance of power shifted. Tongan influence, and then the rise of the great warrior lineages of Upolu and Savaii, eclipsed Manu'a's political supremacy, though the title's sacred aura remained. In the nineteenth century Christianity spread through the islands, the Samoan kingdoms of the main islands contested the chieftainship among themselves, and the powers of Europe and America circled. In 1904 the last Tui Manu'a, Elisara, ceded the Manu'a islands to the United States, and he died in 1909, ending a line remembered as the oldest in Polynesia.
para4: The Samoan chiefdoms endured where the Tui Manu'a did not: the matai system, the village councils, and the fa'a Samoa still order Samoan life today. The memory of Manu'a's ancient sacred kingship, and of the days when Samoan canoes ruled the seas of the southwest Pacific, remains a source of pride in both independent Samoa and American Samoa.
source2label: Samoa News Hub: Reassessing the Tui Manu'a Tradition
